\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{まちどおしい} (machidooshii)}{まちどおしい (machidooshii)}]{\ja{まちどおしい} (machidooshii) — long-awaited}

\label{lesson:JA-C93-machidooshii}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a request, then the Japanese for a desire.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{まちどおしい}}
\textbf{\ja{まちどおしい}} — \emph{machidooshii} — \textquotedblleft{}long-awaited\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{まちどおしい}} (\emph{machidōshii}) is native: \emph{machi}, from \emph{matsu}, \textquotedblleft{}to wait\textquotedblright{}, with \emph{dōshii}, from \emph{tōi}, \textquotedblleft{}far\textquotedblright{}, voiced: the waiting feels far (JMdict). It is inherited rather than borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{ちゅうもん} (chuumon)}{ちゅうもん (chuumon)}]{\ja{ちゅうもん} (chuumon) — an order}

\label{lesson:JA-C93-chuumon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for long-awaited, then the Japanese for a prayer.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{ちゅうもん}}
\textbf{\ja{ちゅうもん}} — \emph{chuumon} — \textquotedblleft{}an order\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{ちゅうもん}} (\emph{chuumon}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{chū}, \textquotedblleft{}pour; note\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{tsyuH}) and \emph{mon}, \textquotedblleft{}writing\textquotedblright{} (\emph{mjun}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription).
\end{cousinweb}
